newsitem.title: UK: Shades of 1994 worry dlr but no model for Fed move.
newsitem.headline: Shades of 1994 worry dlr but no model for Fed move.

text.p: Memories of the dollar's decline after the U.S. embarked on a higher interest rate cycle in 1994 have unsettled traders ahead of an expected rise in U.S. rates this week but analysts are wary of using 1994 as a rule of thumb.

Although higher interest rates are typically viewed as enhancing the return and attractiveness of a country's currency, 1994 proved the reverse. This has left a high degree of uncertainty in the market about the dollar reaction this year.

The Federal Reserve's policy-making Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday and there is widespread speculation it will lift its target for the overnight Federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 5.50 percent.
The Fed funds rate, the rate at which U.S. banks lend to each other on an overnight basis, was last changed in January 1996 when it was lowered by a quarter point to 5.25 percent.

"This is simply not the same situation as 1994," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London. "Back then the Fed tightened after an extreme phase of easy money and the net liquidity shock caused a severe dislocation in bond and stock markets."

After a continuous easing of the funds rate to a record low at 3.0 percent between 1989 and 1994, the Fed reversed a five-year old stance on February 4, 1994. In the months that followed global bond markets collapsed and by the summer the dollar had lost almost 20 pfennigs and 20 yen.
That sort of shock is not likely to be precipitated this time around and the dollar should instead take a positive cue from the more appealing interest rate yield on its head, said Prendergast.

Analysts say the reason the dollar is so vulnerable to the reaction of the bond market is because of the amount of foreign investment in dollar securities, which are needed to fund the huge U.S. current account deficit. When these funds retrench from volatile U.S. asset markets, the dollar shivers.

"You can't take 1994 as a role model for the dollar's reaction to a Fed tightening this time around," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "People are always keen to draw comparisons with 1994 but Fed policy is nearly as expansive now as it was back then."

Prendergast at Merrill said in the latest floating exchange rate period since the early 1970's the dollar has always reacted negatively to major cycles of rising U.S. interest rates -- these starting in the years 1972, 1977, 1987 and 1994.
Conversely it has reacted positively to minor upward adjustments in interest rates between these major cycles, namely in 1980, 1981, 1984 and 1988, he said.

The economic backdrop this time around suggests this is not likely to be a prolonged period of interest rate rises, rather a shot across the bow of potential inflationary pressures which will be limited in scope and execution.

Analysts point out, for example, that market fears three years ago that the Fed had not acted on time to control inflation subsequently proved unfounded. Markets will be more inclined to give the U.S. central bank the benefit of the doubt this time around and the asset market response will be relatively mild.

The initial reaction tomorrow will hinge largely on how the Fed words any accompanying statement. A suggestion that it has already identified rising inflation could cause U.S. stocks and bonds to worry about a further sharp interest rate increases and risk dragging the dollar with them.
Others feel there will be a temptation to book profits on outstanding dollar positions once the widely-expected quarter-point rate rise is confirmed.

"The U.S. interest rate markets are way too bearish and are pricing in a full point rise in rates by the end of the year," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS. "This has got to be corrected lower and I think we could see the dollar suffer a bit initially as a result."
Moreover, the reaction of interest rate expectations in Germany and Japan may be equally as important for dollar/mark and dollar/yen.

"In 1994 the relative slope of German money market curve steepened more than the U.S. because of expectations the Bundesbank would soon raise rates too." said Meggyesi at Deutsche. "This proved totally false then and is highly unlikely this time either."
